Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01149

You can see the weakness of this reply by recalling what we established: a thing’s existence is its individual identity. One identity cannot have two existences. The apparent counterexample of something that lasts also fails. What lasts keeps one identity throughout. The mind’s analysis creates multiple parts, but these belong to time, which is one connected stretch of measured length. The imagination divides it into parts. Those parts make it seem as though the same thing has different relations to different times, but the thing itself remains one through all of them. Time does not come between the thing and itself; it comes between two parts of time, while the thing’s identity remains one through its successive moments.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01150

The second argument is this: if a nonexistent thing could be restored as exactly the same thing, with all the features that make it that individual, then the original time would also have to be restored, since it is one of those features. Time itself can be absent and restored, just like anything else. But this would make the thing both a first beginning and a restoration. A first beginning is its existence in its own time; a restoration is its existence at a second time. The two are opposites. It would also erase the difference between something that begins and something that is restored: the restored thing would count as restored only because it was a first beginning. Each result is impossible.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01151

This argument does not depend on time being what makes an individual unique. It is enough that time, place, position, and similar features help identify it and belong to its individual identity among things of the same kind in different places and times. Someone might object: time cannot be one of the features that makes an individual unique, since a person can remain the same through two different times. That would make the argument absurd.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01152

The reply is that time, place, position, and similar features help us identify an individual because they belong to the particular circumstances in which that individual exists. If the individual were taken outside the limits of one of these features, it would cease to be what it is—as with a particular quality of a person’s bodily state. This does not conflict with the claim that a collection of features that do not make an individual unique cannot by itself make it unique. That claim concerns uniqueness in the sense that a description fits only one thing. Such uniqueness comes from a mode of existence. Here we mean being distinct from other things: matter must be ready to receive an individual existence. In this sense, a group of features, including time, can distinguish it.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01153

An objection is raised against this argument: we need not accept that a thing found in the first time must be a first beginning. That would follow only if the time itself were not restored. The same objection is raised against the claim that restoring time would lead to an endless chain, since there is no difference between the first and the restored time in their nature, existence, or features. The only difference would be that one is earlier and the other later. If so, time would need another time in which to be restored, and the process would continue without end.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01154

Consider this carefully. Each part of time has its own place in the order of events. Being earlier or later, a beginning or an ending, belongs to what that part of time is. For example, being before Friday belongs to Thursday; being after Thursday belongs to Friday. The same applies to each part of time in relation to all the others. Thursday cannot simply be moved to Friday. If it could, Friday would have to be Thursday too, because Thursday’s place in time is part of what makes it Thursday. The restored time would still have its own identity and nature. If we suppose it restored, it would remain a beginning in its actual nature, even while we call it restored. If it were no longer a beginning, it would not be the same time. The objection therefore fails in both its premises and its replies.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01155

The third argument is this: if a nonexistent thing could be restored as exactly the same thing, then a new thing could appear for the first time that matched it in its nature and every feature that marks it as an individual. Like cases should be treated alike, and the existence of an individual with these features is assumed to be possible. But then there would be no difference between the new thing and the restored one, since they would share the same nature and all the same identifying features.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01156

Two objections are raised. First, the things need not be indistinguishable in reality. If they could not be distinguished, they would not be two things; but the mind’s inability to tell them apart does not show that they are indistinguishable in reality. Second, if this argument worked, it would also rule out two similar things appearing for the first time. This would not be an argument about restoring a nonexistent thing at all.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01157

The first reply fails because two things cannot differ in reality unless they differ in some individual feature. If they have no such difference, they are not two things. To say “If they were not different, they would not be two things” simply assumes the very point being disputed. The question is whether, once restoration is allowed, a restored thing and a new thing can both exist without any real difference between them, even though one is restored and the other begins for the first time.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01158

The second reply says that two things alike in every respect may lack any real distinction wherever they appear. But that is not our case. Here, the supposed difference between the two comes only from calling one restored. We are asked to accept a real distinction between them on that basis alone.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01159

Someone might object that they are not wholly indistinguishable: one existed before, while the other did not. But that is precisely the distinction that the argument calls into question. We have already shown that nonexistence is the destruction of the thing itself. A thing that does not exist has no identity, and there is no distinction among things simply as nonexistent. There is only sheer absence. So the subjects of the two existences, and of the nonexistence between them, cannot be one and the same thing: its identity is not preserved through nonexistence.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01160

If the restored thing is distinguished from the new one by an identity that links its two existences across the time when it was absent, then the nonexistent thing would have an identity after all. But it does not. If they are distinguished because one existed earlier, that is just the very relation whose possibility is in question. Both things would have an equal claim to it. Without continuity to make them two moments of one individual, how could one alone be linked to the thing that existed before?
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01161

No one should argue that, for philosophers, a thing’s existence in the mind is like the Muʿtazilite idea of things that remain fixed while nonexistent. Perhaps, they might say, an individual identity could be preserved in some higher form of knowledge, such as God’s knowledge or the Preserved Tablet, beyond the reach of change.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01162

We have already explained that an individual’s mode of existence and identity cannot be preserved while its realm of existence changes. This applies only to general natures, whose different modes of existence and individual features lie outside their meaning. Every mental image, considered in itself, is general: whatever its details, the mind can suppose that it applies to more than one thing. Only some further reason, such as the impossibility of two exact duplicates, may lead the mind to rule out this possibility. So if the same mental image first exists in the outside world and then appears there again, the second is a different individual from the first, because nothing has preserved its individual identity.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01163

An image formed by the senses becomes an image of this particular thing because the senses connect it with the world outside. Imagination, too, singles out its image through what the mind supposes and connects it with. If you picture Zayd, who has died, then set aside what you know about his past life and look closely at the image itself, you will see that it could apply to many people.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01164

The fourth argument is this: an individual thing could be restored only if some part of its complete cause were restored, along with the particular readiness of its matter and the other conditions that complete its cause and make its effect possible. We can ask the same question about the final part of its cause, and about the readiness of the matter for that cause, and continue back through the chain to the highest principles and causes. As will become clear, the conclusion is impossible; so the claim that led to it is impossible too.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01165

The connection is plain. If the cause and the matter’s readiness were not exactly the same as before, the supposed restoration would really be a new beginning, a likeness of the earlier thing. A being could return as the same individual only if all the conditions that made it ready to exist returned too: the cycles of the heavens, the positions of the stars, and everything that came earlier in the whole order of the world, with all its conditions and consequences—even its being a first beginning. A sound nature does not hesitate to reject this idea.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01166

Most theologians who allow nonexistent things to be restored oppose all the philosophers. They think that allowing restoration is what makes bodily resurrection possible, as the religious laws and revealed books say it will be. They do not understand that divine truths cannot be learned through theological debate and argument. There are only two ways to know them. The way of the righteous is to establish the practices of worship, keep to justice, and free oneself from the habits that cloud the mind. Those brought near to God take another path. They develop their understanding and turn their powers of awareness toward what is holy. They polish the soul like a mirror, so that bad character will not stain it, the impressions brought by the senses will not cloud it, and false opinions will not distort it.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01167

Then the truths of faith appear to the soul, which can see what the senses cannot and understand it through its own clear nature. But a soul stained by bad actions, dulled by poor character, or bent by false opinions—as happens to many who make a career of disputation—remains shut off from the truths of faith. It cannot reach God, and it loses the happiness of the next life. As God says, “No indeed! On that Day they will be kept from their Lord.” Whoever hopes to learn through debate and argument about God, His attributes and acts, the sending of messengers and the revelation of books, the next world, life after death, or any of the other mysteries of creation and return has mistaken a swelling for sound flesh. When we come to discuss how souls return to their Maker in the two worlds and reach their Sustainer in both realms, it will become clear how bodily resurrection takes place: souls return to their bodies by permission of the One who brings all things into being, in both their beginning and their return, just as the revealed teachings state.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01168

Although these theologians agree that substances can be restored, they disagree about attributes, or accidents. Some say no accident can ever be restored, since it would have to be restored through another accident, which would make one accident depend on another. Some Ashʿarites hold this view. Most of them say that accidents that do not endure, such as sounds and musical notes, cannot be restored, because they belong only to the times in which they occur. They divide enduring accidents into those within human power and those beyond it. They say that neither a person nor God can restore the first kind, but that God can restore the second. They offer separate proofs for these claims, filling their books with flimsy arguments and other fancies.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01169

Many of their other mistaken views are just as disgraceful. They claim that there are several eternal beings. They say God acts by an arbitrary will with no purpose, and that His creation has no wisdom. They also say He has an inner speech and an imagined conversation, and that things which do not exist are somehow fixed. Finally, they claim that matter is made of indivisible atoms. But that would mean a moving thing is at rest, a millstone comes apart, or an object jumps from one place to another without crossing the space between. These and other tricks and embellishments all come from rejecting wisdom and opposing the philosophers. In truth, these people are innovators who lead others astray, guides for the ignorant and the low-minded. They are a danger to religious and devout people, and a threat to scholars. Among all groups, they are most hostile to the believing philosophers and those who know God.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01170

These quarrelsome debaters plunge into questions of reason without understanding what the senses show us. They attempt proofs and logical arguments without knowing mathematics, and speak about divine things while ignorant of nature.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01171

Most of what they argue over consists of dressed-up claims that have no truth or existence outside their own false imaginings. They can offer no proof when challenged, even about things whose reality most people accept. When pressed, they deny these things rather than admit, “We do not know; God and His Messenger know best.” Yet their language is polished and their expressions elegant. They present false fancies and mistaken beliefs in the clearest words, write them in the neatest hand, and read them aloud to the young and the uneducated. They plant these ideas so deeply in people’s minds that they are almost impossible to remove. Through all this harm and hardship for religious people, they still claim that their weak minds and limited understanding defend Islam and strengthen the faith. To this day, we have not heard of a Jew who turned back through one of them, a Christian who became Muslim, or a Zoroastrian who came to believe. Rather, when people of those faiths see the debaters’ views, they cling to their own religions even more. May God protect the faith and the believers from their harm and corruption.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01172

It is also strange that some of them have used the philosophers’ saying as proof that restoration is possible: “When you hear of wonders in the natural world, leave them within the bounds of possibility unless a clear proof rules them out.” Because they have not trained themselves to reason carefully, they have failed to distinguish two meanings of possibility. One means that the mind has not clearly seen either side as necessary. The other means that a thing is possible in itself: by its own nature, neither its existence nor its nonexistence is necessary. They then assume that anything not proved necessary or impossible must be possible in itself. On this basis, they claim that restoring a nonexistent thing is possible in itself. Many who came later clung to this flimsy and harmful idea, woven by the spider’s web of their own imaginings.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01173

We say to them and their followers: if by “the default” you mean what is common or more likely, it is not clear that most things whose necessity or impossibility has not been proved are possible. Even if they were, this would not help your case. Restoration might be one of the few exceptions. If you mean that a claim should stand unless there is proof against it, as people sometimes argue when interpreting religious law, that rule does not apply here. None of the three ways a thing can be—necessary, possible, or impossible—is a default of this kind. Each follows from the nature of the thing under discussion. If no proof has been given, we simply do not know which applies.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01174

This is what Avicenna meant: when there is no proof that something is necessary, or that it is impossible, we should not deny it or claim that it is impossible. We should leave it within the bounds of possibility—that is, regard it as something reason may consider. He did not mean that we should believe it possible in itself. He also said that anyone who makes a habit of believing things without proof has turned away from human nature.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01175
Chapter — Why nonexistence is not a relation
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01176

The early philosophers held that the connection expressed by a statement is always affirmative, whether the statement says that something is so or says it is not. A negative statement does not create a new connection of its own. It denies the connection asserted by the matching positive statement. It does not join the thing named to what is said about it; it denies that they are joined. We call it a statement that links a description to its subject only by comparing it with a positive statement. For this reason, a negative statement has no separate status based on negation. Its status is the status of the matching affirmative connection. Later philosophers disagreed. They said that a negative statement has its own negative connection, different from an affirmative one, and that it too has a status of its own.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01177

Both affirmative and negative statements fall under three statuses: necessary, impossible, or possible. We usually explain them through affirmative statements because a negative one can be expressed through its positive counterpart. For example, if a thing must be absent, its existence is impossible; if its absence is impossible, its existence is necessary; and if it may be absent, it may also exist. A statement’s status tells us whether what it says about a thing must be true, cannot be true, or may be true.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01178

In a simple statement, such as “A human exists,” the status concerns the thing itself: whether it must exist, cannot exist, or may exist or not. It does not concern a link between that thing and a separate description. In a more complex statement, such as “A human is a writer,” the status concerns whether that description applies to the thing, and how firmly or weakly it does so. A negative statement says either that the thing itself does not exist, or that the description does not apply to it. It does not introduce an entity called “absence,” or a thing that has absence as a feature. So there is no negative connection that could itself have one of the three statuses.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01179
What the early philosophers called a statement’s “element” or “status” is, in a simple statement, the thing’s own condition: whether it must always exist, must always be absent, or may go either way.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01180

In a more complex statement, it is the description’s condition when applied positively to the thing. The difference between possibility and necessity or impossibility is like the difference between weakness and strength, or looseness and firmness. This will become clear in this book and in our way of doing philosophy. If we state a claim’s status in words, that wording can differ from the way things really are. We have now shown that a negative statement has the same status as its corresponding affirmative statement. If the claim were made positively, it would have one of the statuses already described, whether or not anyone actually makes it.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01181

Someone may think that a statement has one status when its predicate is “nonexistent” and another when its predicate is “existent”; or that the status changes when nonexistence, rather than existence, is treated as the link. The mistake is to treat “Zayd is nonexistent” as though it gave Zayd a feature called nonexistence. The intended meaning is simply “Zayd does not exist.” Once we treat the first sentence as a positive claim with a negative description, we have changed what it says. That is why the status of the two statements differs. Whatever idea we take as a predicate has a certain status in its positive relation to a particular subject. That status does not change when the relation is denied.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01182

When we mean to say that Zayd does not exist at all, we should not treat “nonexistent” as a feature that belongs to him. We mean that he himself is absent. Then the statement is a simple negative one. It is not an affirmative statement that attributes the absence of existence to him, nor a compound negative statement that removes existence from a subject that is already there.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01183

Anyone who fails to distinguish simple statements from more complex ones, and assumes that every statement must either attribute something to a subject or deny something of it, will not accept that “A human exists” or “A human came to be” means that the human being himself exists or came to be. They will think instead that it means some feature called existence belongs to him. Likewise, “A human’s nonexistence” means that the human being himself is absent, not that a feature called existence has been removed from him. But “A human is a writer” attributes writing to him, while keeping a person’s fingers still denies the act of writing. Failing to see this difference is a deep-rooted error in human thought, one that must be corrected. Otherwise, people will feel forced to make an exception to the general rule that what is affirmed of a subject depends on the subject’s existence—even in simple statements, as we explained earlier.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01184

Now that you understand that negation, as negation, has no definite content that can be affirmed or denied of something as necessary, impossible, or possible, you can see that there is no negative link that is itself necessary, lasting, actual, or possible. To say that a negative link is necessary means that the corresponding positive link is impossible. To say that a negative link lasts means that the positive link is absent at every time. We consider the status of the affirmative statement, then deny that link for each time under consideration. So, in this refined account, “It is necessarily not the case that this is so” means that the positive claim is impossible; and “This is never so” means that the positive claim fails at every time. This differs from the usual account in general philosophy. The same applies to the other kinds of qualified statements and to unqualified statements, which stand in contrast to them. An unqualified statement has no added mode; its contrast with a qualified one is like the contrast between lacking a feature and having it. An unqualified negative statement is simply a negative statement without any added mode. We cannot separate “an unqualified denial” from “denying that something is qualified.” A full explanation would take us beyond the scope of this book.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01185
Our aim here is to show the way to truth and how to travel toward God. The detailed work belongs to the discipline of logic.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01186
Chapter — Why a negative statement still needs its two terms
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01187

What we say about a thing may or may not exist outside the mind. But to make a judgment, we must have both the thing and what we say about it present in thought. We cannot judge what is not before the mind. The subject, too, must exist in thought in every statement, whether affirmative or negative. If a statement affirms something about the outside world, its subject must also exist there. You cannot affirm one thing of another unless that other thing exists in some way.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01188

There is one exception: what is said may itself mean pure negation, as in “Zayd does not exist outside the mind” or “A partner to God is impossible.” Although these statements seem to speak about the outside world, they deny that anything exists there. In effect, they say: “The Zayd we picture in the mind is not outside it.”
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01189

When a statement denies something about the outside world, the act of denying does not require the thing named to exist there. We may deny something of what does not exist, or deny that an absent thing exists. This is true of negation as negation, not of a judgment made by the human mind, which requires something to be present in thought. So when people say that the subject of a negative statement is broader than the subject of an affirmative statement with a negative description, they do not mean that only the negative statement can be about something that does not exist outside the mind. Affirmative statements can do that too, as in “A partner to God is impossible” or “Contradictions cannot exist together.” Nor do they mean that a subject of an affirmative statement can be present in the mind while the subject of a negative one cannot. Both must be present in thought. They mean that a negative statement can apply to something precisely as absent—as something that has no existence at all. The mind can consider it in that way. An affirmative statement cannot describe it from that same standpoint; it can say something of it only where it has some kind of existence.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01190

That is why one may say that what is wholly nonexistent is nothing and has nothing, so long as one means it in the respect in which it does not exist. We may also deny every positive feature of a subject precisely as absent. But we cannot affirm some other feature of it from that same standpoint. The exception is when the feature named is itself negative or impossible: then the statement can be true without requiring the subject to exist in that respect, even though an affirmative link normally requires some existence. This is why people have said that the subject of a negative statement is broader than the subject of an affirmative one. That wording is misleading unless understood in the way just explained. It does not mean that a negative statement may have a subject that is absent outside the mind while an affirmative statement may not.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01191

Some argue that if the subject of a negative statement is broader than the subject of an affirmative statement with a negative description, the two statements cannot contradict each other, because they would apply to different things. But if the subject is not broader, they say, then there is no difference between the statements.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01192

The answer depends on what “broader” means. It may mean that a statement covers more things. Or it may mean that we can consider the same thing in more than one way. Here it means the second, not the first. The two statements need not apply to different individuals. Here it means only the second. So the difference does not break the contradiction between the statements. A negative statement can apply to a subject under a broader description even when it does not cover more actual cases. An affirmative statement is narrower in this respect, though the two may happen to cover the same cases. This is because every concept and every fixed reality is present in the higher levels of existence, and every judgment requires the subject to be present in thought. Something wholly unknown cannot be denied or affirmed. We can also answer the objection by remembering the difference between the two ways of making a statement: something may be denied of itself in one way and affirmed of itself in another.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01193

This difference applies only to statements about particular things or kinds. It does not apply to statements such as “Every G is B,” because that form already includes a positive assumption about its subject: anything described as G, in thought or in reality, with or without a qualifier, is B.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01194

There are more puzzles here, and they can hold back someone on the path toward God. One is that a negative statement with a negative description seems broader than the matching affirmative statement, because it can be true when its subject does not exist. Sometimes the negation of a broad idea has no real example at all, as with “not a thing,” “not known,” or “not possible in general.” Then the rules of logic seem to fail. The negation of a narrower idea may be true of something where the negation of a broader idea is also true, simply because the subject is absent.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01195

This would make a statement such as “It is not the case that some non-substance is non-animal” true just because no such subject exists. The same problem seems to arise with “Some non-body is not non-spatial.” That, too, could be true simply because the subject does not exist. These cases appear to upset the rule that the negation of a narrower idea applies more broadly than the negation of a broader idea. They also seem to undermine the rule that the negations of two ideas with the same scope have the same scope, along with other rules of logic.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01196

These objections seem to undermine not only the rule for reversing an “all” statement through its opposite, but other rules of logic as well. The usual reply is to treat a negative statement as a positive statement that says the predicate does not apply. Its defenders then set apart positive statements with a negative description. They say these do not require the subject to exist, and group them with negative statements. They also set aside rules that concern the negations of very broad ideas. All these replies are reckless guesses by later imitators of the philosophers, people without a firm grounding in knowledge or insight.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01197

The right way to untie the knot is the distinction we made earlier. A negative statement has a broader subject than its matching affirmative statement only in how the mind considers it, not in the number of actual things it covers. This does not mean that one statement can be true of an individual when the other is false of that same individual in the same respect. It means that one can be true of something under one way of considering it, while the other is not true of it under that same way—even though in both cases the subject must exist in some sense.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01198

Every affirmative statement, whether it uses a negative description or a plain one, requires the subject to be established in some way: in the outside world, in thought, or by supposition. Every statement requires some kind of existence. The truth of a negative statement rests on the opposite condition: its subject is taken as assumed or supposed. This resolves the difficulty. Such claims are truly valid, and their subject need exist only as assumed. What makes the statement true is that if something were to fit the description named as its subject, the description named as its predicate would fit it too.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01199

The relation between ideas—whether one applies more broadly, more narrowly, or to the same range as another—does not mean that they must apply together to some actual thing. This is clear in the general idea to which such rules apply: it need not have an example in the outside world or even in the mind.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01200

For example, anything possible in the strict sense is also possible in the broad sense. But anything that is not possible in the strict sense is possible in the broad sense too: it must either exist or be impossible, and both count as possible in the broad sense. If the opposite of what is broadly possible were always narrower than the opposite of what is possible in the strict sense, the first rule would imply that anything not broadly possible is not strictly possible; the second would then imply that the same thing is broadly possible. That is a contradiction. The same contradiction follows if we reverse the two steps.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01201

The philosopher al-Tusi replies that broad possibility divides into two cases that are mutually exclusive and cover every possibility: either one side is necessary—existence or nonexistence—or neither side is necessary. If we take broad possibility to include both cases, then denying broad possibility falls outside the two opposite sides of the contradiction.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01202

Now consider the two arguments just given. The first argument uses the same phrase in two different senses. In one statement, “not strictly possible” lies outside both sides of the opposition; in the other, it falls within one of them. Because the meaning changes, the argument fails.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01203

The second argument also fails. Its first statement is false. The correct reversal of “Everything that is not strictly possible is broadly possible” is not “Everything that is not broadly possible is strictly possible.” It is “Everything that is not broadly possible is not not strictly possible,” meaning again what lies outside both sides of the contradiction, not strict possibility itself.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01204

Someone might object that what lies outside both sides—what we call “nothing”—is not a thing at all. Nothing can be said of it, so how could it be broader than anything? The answer is twofold: “not strictly possible” can apply both to this “nothing” and to what falls under one of the two sides of the contradiction, namely what must exist and what cannot exist. That is all we mean by calling it broader.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01205

A leading philosopher has clarified the issue this way. Broad possibility means that it is not necessary for a thing to be absent. This denies that the opposite side must be true. The opposite side may be the absence of a link between subject and predicate, if possibility concerns their relation; or it may be the subject’s own nonexistence, if “possible” is what we say of the subject itself. Since a thing’s necessary absence would make it impossible, broad possibility means either that the subject itself is not impossible, or that the description applied to it is not impossible. In either case, something impossible in itself is not broadly possible.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01206

Most logicians use “opposite side” to mean whichever of existence or nonexistence goes against the actual state of things. For something necessary, the opposite is nonexistence; for something impossible, it is existence. Broad possibility can then apply to either one. If “broad possibility” means what this philosopher first described, the claim that something impossible in itself is broadly possible is false.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01207

If instead we mean broad possibility as most people do, there are two ways to understand the necessity involved. We may say that each of the necessary and the impossible requires one side only. Then what is not strictly possible falls into three groups: what must exist, what cannot exist, and what must both exist and not exist. In that case, we cannot say that something necessary on both sides lacks necessity on the side that does not occur.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01208

Or we may say that each requires one side without asking whether the other side is also necessary or not. Then we still cannot say that every impossible thing lacks necessity on the side that does not occur, because something necessary on both sides would count as impossible, and yet it would not lack that necessity.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01209

The author of Durrat al-Taj tried to challenge the claim that anything not strictly possible is broadly possible. He argued that if we consider a nature entirely by itself, it is neither strictly possible nor broadly possible. This objection does not work. The claim concerns how things stand in reality, not how the mind views them at one particular level.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01210
Chapter — Can God have a particular kind of nonexistence?
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01211

Philosophers commonly say that some particular ways of existing are impossible for God, whose existence depends on nothing. This does not conflict with His necessary existence. In the same way, a particular way of existing can be impossible for something that depends on another, without contradicting its basic possibility. It may even confirm it. Particular kinds of absence can also be impossible for something dependent, or for something impossible in itself—for example, an absence that comes after existence.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01212

It is clear that God cannot exist in any of the dependent ways of existing: He cannot come into being, pass away, have a body, exist inside another thing, or be a feature of it. These ways involve limits and lack. Some ways of existing are impossible for certain dependent things, and others are impossible for all of them. Existence that depends on nothing is impossible for every dependent thing. Existence as a substance is impossible for a feature; existence apart from matter is impossible for a material thing; and lasting, fixed existence is impossible for something whose being flows from moment to moment.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01213

So a thing that exists only through change cannot, by its very nature, have a time before its existence when it was absent, then appear after that absence, or later become absent after it existed. These “before” and “after” relations belong to time. This does not mean that existence or nonexistence in general is impossible for such a thing. Likewise, once a real existence has taken place, a particular kind of absence that would remove it from reality—given its time, place, or qualities—is impossible for anything that depends on another. This is impossible as a feature of the thing, not by its nature.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01214
Critique and clarification
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01215

There is no doubt that ways of existing that involve limits cannot belong to God. But it is open to question whether a particular way of existing is impossible for Him simply because it is existence. Existence, taken as existence, is one simple reality. Its levels differ only in fullness or lack, strength or weakness. Lack and weakness amount to absence. Each level below God therefore has two sides: it is existence, and it falls short of complete perfection. Insofar as such a level falls short of perfection, it cannot belong to God. But insofar as it is existence, it must belong to Him, for He is necessary in every respect.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01216

If one way of existing were impossible for God simply because it is existence, then His own reality would include both necessity and impossibility. That would make His being a combination of different sides. Someone might object that the same applies to His necessary existence and the impossibility of His nonexistence. But those two descriptions do not point to different things. One reality is the source of both descriptions: its existence is the very reason its absence is impossible. There is no difference in reality or in thought. This is unlike the case we are discussing, where the same reality would stand in two conflicting relations to existence.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01217
This principle supports what we have said: all existing things depend on God. They are flows of His existence, like rays and gifts from the divine reality.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01218

It is also open to question whether particular kinds of absence can be impossible for something that is dependent, or for something impossible in itself. Absence has no distinct kinds, as we have explained. These descriptions of absence may follow from features of existence. For something impossible in itself, an absence that comes after existence is impossible only because the earlier existence is impossible. If the earlier existence cannot happen, then no later absence can follow it. That later absence is impossible only because it depends on the impossible existence. So any kind of absence that belongs to something impossible is impossible because of something else, not in itself.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01219

Here is a well-known puzzle that people have found difficult. If time cannot have an earlier or later absence by its very nature, then time must exist necessarily, just as God does. The common reply is that only God cannot have any kind of absence. Time, they say, could be entirely absent, from beginning to end, so there is no contradiction in time being absent before and after its existence.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01220

But this reply does not fit their own principles. Even if time could be entirely absent, it would still follow that the time that lies between earlier and later absence must exist necessarily. Then it would not need a cause in order to continue existing. Yet, on their own account, something whose existence depends on another needs a cause both to begin and to continue existing.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01221

They try another reply. The opposite of an earlier or later absence, they say, is simply the denial of that absence. But that denial may be true whether time exists continuously or is completely absent from beginning to end. So they claim that the answer does not prove time must exist.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01222

With God’s help, we can avoid these strained replies. In our account, what is necessary in itself is existence without limit. What is impossible in itself is what cannot have existence in any way. A general nature can exist through any one of its examples, and it is absent only if all its examples are absent. But existence is not general in the same way as an abstract idea. It has an openness and reach that the deeply learned understand.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01223

The necessity of the complete reality of existence means that all its levels and forms must exist. Its impossibility would mean that every one of its levels and forms is impossible. Time, with its continuous flow, is one expression of the First Cause and a weak level in the unfolding of existence. It is among the weakest things that depend on another for their existence, and among the lowest in rank of the things we know.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01224

There is another answer to the last objection. Time and motion exist by changing from moment to moment. They do not last as fixed things. Their whole existence is a process of coming to be, moment by moment. This is true whether the movement has an end, like the straight movement of the elements, or continues without end, like the circular movements of the heavens. So it makes no sense to ask whether time needs a cause to keep existing: it has no separate state of continued existence apart from its coming to be.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01225

There is also another way to answer. Time and motion are unlike ordinary features that belong to a thing. Motion is the process of seeking a perfection, whether through a natural tendency or a deliberate choice. It is not a separate thing in its own right. What exists is what is sought, or what can be sought. Time is the measure of that seeking.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01226

As long as we mean time and motion in this way, we cannot ask directly whether either one exists necessarily or possibly, lasts or ends. Such descriptions apply to them only because of something else. If we stop considering them in this way, they are no longer time or motion; they have become something else with different rules.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01227
Chapter — What depends on something impossible in itself need not itself be impossible
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01228

If something depends on what is impossible in itself, that does not mean the dependent thing is impossible in itself. It is impossible because of something else: the thing it depends on is impossible in itself. Someone might say the case is different when what is depended on is the subject—the thing that is impossible in itself—and what depends on it is a property, such as its being impossible in itself. Then the subject's impossibility in itself would entail that the property is impossible in itself too. They say this follows from the special relation between a subject and the property that describes it.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01229

I think that view comes from confusing two kinds of description. Saying that something exists, or does not exist, is not like saying that a thing can receive a quality, or that it lacks that quality. Nor is it like describing an absent thing as lacking a quality it could have received. In those cases, the quality must follow the thing it describes, whether that thing exists or not.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01230

For example, a body must exist before we can describe it as white or not white. The body has its own existence, and the whiteness or lack of whiteness is another fact that follows from it. Only after the body itself exists can we describe it by that quality. The same distinction applies when we speak of a body's absence and the absence of whiteness: one does not simply amount to the other.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01231

Existence works differently. To say that existence belongs to a thing and to say that the thing exists are one and the same: the thing's existence is its own existence. There is no separate quality attached to it. The distinction between the thing and existence is made only in thought, as we explained earlier. The same is true of nonexistence. For a thing not to exist means that it is absent in itself; it does not mean that some other thing is absent from it.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01232

So when we say that existence is necessary, this is the same as saying that the thing that exists is necessary. In reality, neither depends on the other; they differ only in how we consider them. The same is true when we say that a thing's nonexistence is impossible: that is simply to say that the thing that does not exist is impossible.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01233

The same pattern continues when we describe that necessity as necessary again, or say that the impossibility itself must hold. We can keep doing this only as long as we keep extending the analysis in thought. In each case, describing the subject by one of these properties is the same as describing the property itself, or something that follows from it. There is no real dependence between them, and neither comes before the other.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01234

Our conclusion is this: anything that depends on what is impossible in itself is always impossible because of something else, not impossible in itself. It is impossible because it depends on that thing, not because it is that thing. In the same way, anything that is necessary because of something else is possible in itself; it is neither necessary nor impossible in itself, as we have already shown.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01235

Later, we will see that the familiar claim that one impossible thing entails another is not always true. It is true only when there is a rational link between them, as there is between what is impossible in itself and what is impossible because of something else—that is, something that depends on what is impossible in itself. Two things that are each impossible in themselves do not entail one another, just as two things that are each necessary in themselves do not. Nor does a thing entail its opposite.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01236

Why? For one thing to entail another, one must depend on the other. Either one causes the other, or both are caused by something else. So at least one of them must be caused by something else. But anything caused by another is possible in itself, because a thing needs something else only if it is possible in itself. So what is impossible because of something else is possible in itself. Two things that are impossible in themselves do not entail one another, and neither does a thing entail what opposes it.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01237
A seeming problem, and its answer
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01238

Someone might object: if the idea of something possible or impossible does not entail its opposite, how do proofs by assuming the opposite work? They establish something by assuming that it is false, then showing that the assumption leads to a contradiction. For example, to show that time has no beginning or end, they say that if it were absent before it existed, that earlier absence and its later existence could not be together. They make the same argument about its absence after it exists. And to show that spatial magnitudes are finite, they say that an unlimited magnitude would have to be limited.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01239

If you mean that these proofs show that, if the supposedly impossible thing were real, its opposite would also be real—or that if time really were absent before or after it existed, it would not be absent at that time—then the proofs would be false. If those assumptions were real, they would have the consequences and effects that belong to them. They would not contradict themselves or produce effects that oppose them.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01240

But if you mean that these proofs show what follows when we assume one of these things while leaving all the other actual and possible conditions in place, then that is what they do. The assumption, combined with those other conditions, leads to a contradiction: it makes the thing and its opposite both true, or makes the thing both absent and present. That does not mean the thing itself entails its opposite. It means that assuming it, while keeping the other conditions in place, leads to the opposite of what those conditions require. On closer inspection, the assumption amounts to placing two incompatible things together.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01241

In short, a proof of this kind treats something as a supposition, not as something that has actually happened. It assumes the thing and then shows that, together with what follows from it, the assumption leads to its opposite. If we treated it as real, we would also have to accept all that follows from it and everything it depends on. We would have to set aside whatever contradicts it, its consequences, or the things it depends on. Only then would we be treating it as a real state of affairs.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01242

But that is not what the proof does. It says: if we assume this thing and think through what follows, we find its opposite. It does not say: if this thing were really the case, its absence would also be real. The supposed impossible thing, considered as an idea in the mind, leads to the idea of a contradiction. But two conflicting ideas can be considered together in the mind. As we have noted, they are possible as ideas.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01243

The proof then shows that the conclusion it draws does not stand for anything that exists in the world of possible things. So it argues from the absence of that conclusion to the falsehood of the original assumption. The conditional claim and the denial of its conclusion together show that the assumption is impossible; the assumption alone does not.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01244

Take note: we established earlier that what is necessary in itself cannot be necessary because of something else. Apply the same reasoning to what is impossible in itself. It cannot also be impossible because of something else. Otherwise, its own impossibility would disappear if that other thing disappeared.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01245

Also, one thing cannot have two nonexistences or two impossibilities. Nor can one nonexistence and one impossibility belong to two different things. By contrast, one thing can have two existences or two necessities, and two different things can share an existence or a necessity. This shows that existence and nonexistence, and the necessity of existing or not existing, multiply only when their subjects do.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01246

It is therefore impossible for the same thing to be impossible in itself and impossible because of something else, either at once or at different times. What is impossible in itself is impossible through its own nature alone.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01247

We have now seen that anything made necessary or impossible by something else is possible in itself. We have also seen that possibility in itself must be understood so that it can become either necessary or impossible because of something else, as something incomplete can be brought to completion. That is why a possible thing can take on either description.
Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence
passage-en-01248

Remember that the human mind cannot bear the radiance of the First Reality, God, or grasp the full reality of His glory and majesty. His light, perfection, and actuality are too great. In the same way, the mind cannot grasp what is impossible in itself, because it falls so far short of existence that it is not even a thing. A thing cannot be separated from existence; what does not exist is not a thing.
